Introducing AMD Helion, Agentic AI Compute at Rack Scale :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
Introducing AMD Helion, Agentic AI Compute at Rack Scale
October 12, 2026 9:00 am EDT
Download as PDF
News Highlights:
AMD Helion lets customers tailor CPU core density, performance and power to agentic workloads, with CPU-only configurations for hyperscale deployments and integrated CPU/GPU configurations for enterprises.
AMD Helion combines open hardware and software with an integrated token router that directs agents’ model calls across frontier and open-source models.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Oct.  12, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) --
AMD
(NASDAQ: AMD) today introduced the AMD Helion agentic AI rack, an open blueprint for agentic AI infrastructure based on an Open Compute Project spec-design and powered by AMD compute.
Building on the open-platform approach of the AMD Helios™ rackscale solution, AMD Helion is designed to provide partners and customers with the flexibility they need for agentic AI infrastructure. With AMD Helion, customers can match CPU performance, core density and power with GPU acceleration for the work their AI agents perform.
“Agentic AI is not a single workload. It spans personal agents, enterprise applications, code execution and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements,” said Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD. “To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD EPYC™ performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power.”
AMD Helion’s OCP spec-based rack blueprint supports open software and can come in flexible configurations, including liquid- and air-cooled versions, allowing customers to create virtually any configuration needed for their needs. Some examples of this include:
A CPU-only rack powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors that can support up to 32,768 CPU cores. This rack is designed for hyperscale customers, providing dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure.
An all-in-one rack that combines AMD EPYC CPU nodes, AMD Instinct™ MI350P GPU nodes and general-purpose compute on one platform. This rack is designed to provide partners and customers an all-in-one concept for enterprise agentic AI.
AMD Helion enables customers to deploy agentic AI in the IT infrastructure they already have, turning existing investments into a foundation for new AI capabilities. Partners can tailor CPU and GPU configurations to customer workloads, matching agent execution, model inference and supporting compute to each deployment’s performance, power and cost requirements.
AMD plans to contribute the AMD Helion specification to OCP, making it available to the community for further development and adoption. AMD Helion agentic rack configurations are currently under development with ecosystem partners and are planned to be available in November 2026.
Ecosystem Support
AMD is helping shape the next phase of AI infrastructure through open, flexible platforms, a broad portfolio of workload-optimized compute and collaboration across the ecosystem. AMD Helion brings that approach to agentic AI, helping partners match software and compute to the work agents perform and giving customers flexibility to scale as their requirements evolve.
“Agentic AI is changing what customers need from their infrastructure. It's not just about compute performance, but how the entire system is connected, managed and secured. Architectures like AMD Helion, combined with Cisco's full-stack infrastructure capabilities, can give customers greater flexibility to deploy, operate and scale agentic workloads into their environments as their needs evolve.” -
Jeremy Foster, Senior Vice President and General Manager, Cisco Compute
“Dell PowerRack gives customers choice without compromise, and our support for AMD Helion Agentic Rack Reference Design extends that promise to the next generation of agentic AI. By combining AMD's rack-scale architecture with Dell's proven engineering expertise, along with the flexibility to extend deployments with Dell PowerRack for Networking and Storage, we're giving customers a complete, validated path to deploy agentic compute at scale with the manageability and reliability they expect from Dell.” -
Arun Narayanan, Senior Vice President, Compute and Networking, Dell Technologies
“Hon Hai Technology Group continues to deepen its collaboration with AMD on AI infrastructure, supporting the new AMD Helion Agentic AI Rack reference design. Built on an open architecture, the platform combines 6th Gen AMD EPYC processors with flexible CPU and GPU configurations to address hyperscale data center and enterprise Agentic AI workloads. The Group will continue to leverage its strengths in rack-level system integration and global manufacturing, working with ecosystem partners to advance rack-scale Agentic AI solutions and accelerate next-generation AI infrastructure deployment.” –
Hon Hai Technology Group
“Next-generation AI workloads require scale, efficiency, and flexibility that open, rack-scale architectures deliver, as demonstrated by our recent customer agreement to deploy AMD Helios. For decades, HPE and AMD have jointly championed open standards, and we are continuing to advance those efforts with AMD Helion. Together, we are ushering in the next era of AI with open large-scale systems, enhanced with air-cooled and direct liquid-cooled networking, supported by decades of HPE expertise and innovation.” –
Trish Damkroger, Senior Vice President and General Manager, HPC & AI Infrastructure Solutions, HPE
“As agentic AI moves into production, customers need flexibility in how and where they deploy it. That’s at the core of the Lenovo Hybrid AI Advantage, and AMD Helion will give added versatility to meet customers where they are and support the workloads they want to run.” -
Scott Patti, VP, Infrastructure Solutions Group, Lenovo
“Agentic AI will require a range of system designs to serve different customer needs. AMD Helion provides an open blueprint that gives QCT the flexibility to tailor compute configurations and bring system design and customization expertise to those requirements.” - Mike Yang, President of QCT
“Supermicro is accelerating the deployment of next-generation agentic AI infrastructure by bringing AMD’s Helion - the open, ORv3 compliant rack-scale architecture to market through our Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS). With our proven expertise in OCP accepted™ rack-scale design, integration, liquid cooling, software, and deployment services, we transform advanced Agentic AI architectures into production-ready solutions. Together with AMD, we enable customers to deploy faster, scale efficiently, and accelerate time to online for agentic AI.” -
Vik Malyala, Chief Business Officer, Supermicro
“AMD Helion provides an open, flexible foundation for agentic AI infrastructure. Wiwynn is excited to collaborate with AMD, bringing our expertise in rack-level integration and advanced cooling to help hyperscaler customers tailor systems that meet the demanding workloads, power requirements, and data center environments of the agentic AI era.” -
William Lin, President and CEO, Wiwynn

Skip to footer
Try Claude
Announcements
2026 Usage Policy update
Oct 8, 2026
Each year, Anthropic updates its Usage Policy in response to the evolving capabilities of our models, and the feedback we’ve received from our customers. We're publishing a new version of the policy today. In this post, we summarize the changes we’ve made.
Most of the updates in the latest version are intended to clarify existing rules. In the year since our last refresh, Claude has taken on longer, more independent work. This update provides new examples that show how our rules apply to Claude’s new capabilities. It draws on new patterns of misuse in influence operations, weapons development, and surveillance that we’ve observed in the past year (as we’ve documented in our
latest threat intelligence report
). We’ve also made updates to clarify our requirements for high-risk use cases in areas like health and finance, to add controls for when Claude is used to autonomously take physical actions, and to address abusive behavior toward our models.
The updated policy takes effect on November 12. The full
Usage Policy
and
Supported Regions Policy
can be found on their respective pages.
A new section on deceptive activity
As we
wrote about last month
, we’ve seen examples of state media outlets, government propaganda offices, and commercial firms using Claude to run networks of fake accounts and fabricated news sites. Our policy already prohibited this activity, but the restrictions were scattered across our elections, fraud, privacy, and disinformation sections.
We've consolidated those rules into a new section titled Do Not Engage in Deceptive Campaigns or Artificial Activity, which applies to deceptive activity of any kind (whether political or commercial). It covers efforts to obscure who is behind a message or amplify content through fake accounts or posts, along with building the tools and infrastructure for running influence operation campaigns.
Refocusing our elections section
We’ve refined our political content restrictions in each version of our Usage Policy in order to ensure that our models can be used appropriately in democratic processes. In this version, we’ve further sharpened our section on elections, focusing it specifically on disallowing the use of Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections (for instance, by spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, or trying to suppress turnout). We’ve renamed it Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes to reflect that scope.
For a similar reason, we’ve also removed our blanket prohibition on personalized vote and campaign targeting. This prohibition covered legitimate civic work, such as nonprofits using Claude to write information for voters in other languages, or election officials sending ballot cure notices. The behaviors that motivated the original rule (like voter targeting that relies on deception or the misuse of voters’ personal data) remain prohibited under our deceptive campaigns, surveillance, and privacy sections.
Clarifying our weapons prohibitions
Our Usage Policy has always prohibited using Claude to develop weapons. Recently, we’ve seen people attempt to use our models to build guidance and control software for weapons. The updated section makes clear that our prohibitions include the software and components that make weapons work, as well as actions like arming drones and other autonomous vehicles. These changes reflect how we’ve enforced our previous policy.
More precise language on surveillance and law enforcement
Our September
threat intelligence report
documented the growing use of AI to build surveillance systems that identify and track political dissidents. We’ve rewritten our surveillance and criminal justice section to state more precisely what we prohibit. For instance, tracking people without their consent is prohibited, whether it happens in real time or through analysis of previously collected data. Claude cannot be used to decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest, or charge in a law enforcement or criminal justice process. We also prohibit Claude from being used to build or improve tools designed for surveillance.
As with the previous update to our weapons prohibitions, this update does not reflect a change in what we enforce in practice: it is just intended to make our policy more explicit. The new section also spells out which uses remain permitted, including tracking that people have agreed to (such as fraud monitoring), content moderation, journalism, and legal research.
Clearer requirements for high-risk use cases
When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified “human in the loop” (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.
These requirements haven’t changed with the updated version of our Usage Policy. However, users have often asked us whether a given use case has these requirements, so we've rewritten our High-risk Use Case Requirements section to answer that more directly. It now lists which kinds of recommendations are covered and which are not.
Following the launch of our
Model Hardware Standard
, this section also adds requirements for the use of our models when they’re connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury. A qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed; the equipment must also be able to hold a safe state if Claude is disconnected.
Addressing abusive behavior toward our models
We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.
This addition aligns with a step we've already taken, allowing Claude models to
end rare conversations with persistently abusive users
on Claude.ai and Claude Code. Such abuse is the main focus of this update; Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism.
Clarifying our Supported Regions Policy
Last year, we
updated our Supported Regions Policy
to restrict access to Claude for companies who are majority-owned by entities headquartered in our unsupported regions. We've updated our
Supported Regions page
to clarify how we enforce this policy. Our policy prohibits the use of Claude by people who are physically located in an unsupported region, by entities who are incorporated or headquartered in one, and by entities who are majority-owned or controlled by persons or entities in those regions.
Looking ahead
We'll keep updating our Usage Policy as Claude’s capabilities and risks change. As with this and our prior updates, we’ll seek input from across Anthropic, and from policymakers, subject matter experts, civil society, and the people who use our products.

Building on our commitment to American scientific discovery
Oct 8, 2026
Anthropic is deepening its support for American scientific research by committing $150 million over three years to the
Genesis Mission
, a federal initiative to accelerate scientific and technological discovery through AI. The funding will go toward making Claude available to more than 15 agencies that are part of the mission, including NASA, the National Institutes of Health, and the National Science Foundation.
We first announced our partnership with the US Department of Energy (DOE) and the Genesis Mission
last December
. Since then, we have
worked with
DOE to bring Claude to scientists across the national laboratories. Today, we announced this new commitment as part of the Science: A New Golden Age Summit hosted by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy in Washington, DC.
Supporting American scientists
We share the administration’s view, laid out in “
Science: A New Golden Age
,” that AI can have a profound and positive impact on scientific discovery, and we are glad to back its efforts to support American scientists.
Researchers at federal agencies and national laboratories work on some of the world’s most difficult scientific problems. Through our commitment, we aim to help them use Claude to meaningfully advance their work. Over the next three years, we will:
Provide Claude, Claude Code, and API credits to several hundred Genesis Mission research projects;
Partner closely with agencies and national laboratories on the administration’s top science priorities, including fusion energy and quantum computing; and
Provide training, onboarding, and technical support to scientists on Genesis Mission projects, and
help agencies new to the Genesis Mission get their first projects running.
Accelerating scientific research
This commitment is part of our broader effort to support scientific research. Earlier this year we launched
Claude Science
, an AI workbench that integrates the tools and packages researchers most commonly use, and
opened 10,000 free and discounted Claude seats
for academic scientists. We also expanded our
AI for Science
program, which gives credits to researchers on high-impact projects, and kicked off a research preview of the
Model Hardware Standard
, a shared specification for AI agents to safely operate lab instruments. Our commitment to the Genesis Mission is our next step toward helping researchers everywhere.

Introducing the Anthropic Cyber Mission \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Skip to footer

Announcements
Introducing the Anthropic Cyber Mission
Oct 8, 2026
Today we’re launching the Anthropic Cyber Mission, a long-term commitment to securing the systems everyone depends on. The Cyber Mission is a new effort to support defenders with tools, research, and resources to secure their software and systems. We’re starting with two areas:
Critical infrastructure:
Starting with securing the operational technology behind power grids, water systems, and transportation networks, and protecting government systems. Today, we’re introducing the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program (CIDP), which brings frontier models, on-site engineers, and threat research to the defenders that protect operational technology.
Open-source software:
Finding vulnerabilities and proposing patches in the free, shared code that most software depends on, and hardening the underlying code. Today, we’re launching
OSS Scanner
, which offers open-source projects regular security scans from our strongest models, for free.
Frontier models can be misused to exploit vulnerabilities and conduct cyber operations. Despite best efforts, many areas of technology remain dangerously exposed. State-sponsored adversaries have spent years gaining footholds in these systems, across many sectors, so that they can disrupt them. Defenders of critical infrastructure and the OSS community have decades of security experience but have faced severe resource shortages that are exacerbated by this moment. We are recognizing their expertise in these domains and offering our support. We will also expand the Cyber Mission to release tools, research, and resources in new areas to help secure the world.
As part of
Project Glasswing
, partners uncovered many vulnerabilities, but we haven’t yet achieved a sufficient reduction in cyber risk. It’s easier than ever to find vulnerabilities, but verifying, prioritizing, and fixing these findings remains challenging. Based on lessons from Project Glasswing, we’re starting these new efforts to support defenders. Earlier this week, we merged Project Glasswing into our expanded
Cyber Verification Program
, which gives many more defenders access to our most capable models. And through the Anthropic Cyber Mission, we’ll deploy Anthropic engineering talent and provide tools and funding for those who secure critical infrastructure and open-source software.
Defending critical infrastructure
Power grids, water utilities, factories, and transportation networks run on controllers, control software, and industrial networks built to last for decades. These systems are known as “operational technology,” and they often cannot be taken offline to patch, so known vulnerabilities can stay unresolved for years. Securing them is specialized work: the equipment is proprietary, changes are risky, and a mistake can take down a plant. Operators of every size rely on a small set of trusted providers to support that work, telling them what’s exposed and which fixes to make on a running system.
Today, we’re introducing the
Critical Infrastructure Defense Program
, which brings frontier Claude models, on-site engineers, and our threat research to those trusted providers. Its founding partners are Accenture, Booz Allen, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC, and Rockwell Automation.
These organizations represent the providers that operators rely on to secure these systems: the consulting and advanced technology companies that run security programs, the security companies that guard the business and industrial networks, and the manufacturers that build and patch the equipment itself.
This work is underway. Several partners are currently working with Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same. Critical infrastructure is hard to defend in many ways that AI cannot fix, but we believe that frontier models can help find and repair weaknesses before those weaknesses are used to cut off power or make water unsafe. Our first step is to work with a small cohort of providers to learn which strategies are most effective and practical.
If your company builds security products or services for critical infrastructure, you can
register your interest here
.
As AI continues to advance, it presents an important opportunity to strengthen cybersecurity across critical infrastructure, provided it is applied responsibly, validated rigorously, and deployed with safety and reliability at the forefront. We are pleased to contribute our operational technology and industrial cybersecurity expertise to help develop practical approaches for applying AI in ways that strengthen the resilience of the infrastructure society depends on every day.
Through our work with critical infrastructure organizations, PwC’s cyber OT practice has seen firsthand the gravity of consequences cyber breaches can have in these environments. I firmly believe that a coordinated, industry-wide effort is necessary to identify vulnerabilities, mitigate risks, and strengthen the resilience of our critical systems.
Threat actors are using AI to find and exploit exposures at machine speed. By combining Unit 42 threat intelligence and operational expertise with Anthropic’s frontier models, we’re helping operators defend against adversaries looking to attack and disrupt essential services. Together, we are giving defenders the speed and precision needed to close attack paths before exposure becomes impact.
Frontier AI is evolving faster than any single organization can track alone. That’s why the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program matters. It brings together the people who understand these environments with the frontier capabilities now available to defend them. We’re proud to contribute our experience and to learn alongside the other partners working to protect the systems the world depends on.
The sites that need protection most, like remote substations, offshore platforms, and air-gapped plants, are exactly where traditional tools can’t reach and specialists can’t be. What no one had solved was the hours: more data than any team can work through, at more sites than any team can staff. Claude closes that gap, so our analysts and our customers’ operators spend their time on the judgment calls that keep critical systems running safely.
Critical infrastructure and the people who depend on it benefit when the vendor community shares what they learn about the opportunities and challenges that AI presents to operational environments, rather than keeping that knowledge in silos. Joining Anthropic's Critical Infrastructure Defense Program is one of the ways we help align frontier AI to a collective defense strategy built around the realities of the operational technology (OT) that keeps the lights on, water safe, and transportation running.
Critical infrastructure is where cyber risk becomes real-world risk. As adversaries use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale, critical infrastructure facing machine-speed threats requires machine-speed defense. By bringing CrowdStrike’s deep security context and expertise together with Anthropic’s frontier AI expertise, we can put a greater advantage in the hands of critical infrastructure defenders.
Amid the rapid evolution of AI and the increasing sophistication and speed of cyber threats, ensuring cybersecurity in OT environments that support social infrastructure has become one of the highest priorities facing society today. Through participation in this program, we look forward to collaborating with Anthropic and fellow partners to further enhance cyber resilience for critical infrastructure.
As AI accelerates, critical infrastructure operators need solutions that address security vulnerabilities at machine speed. Together with Anthropic, Deloitte is helping provide these enterprises with the enablement needed to close security gaps and strengthen resilience, moving at pace with the realities of frontier AI.
Operational technology is the next frontier for autonomous AI-enabled attacks. The question is no longer whether AI can affect an industrial process, but how much control it can gain, and how quickly. The Critical Infrastructure Defense Program is convening the best of private-sector innovation and investment to strengthen OT and ICS resilience across federal and commercial missions.
Organizations that keep our power on, medicine safe, food supply secure, and communications running face some of the most consequential cyber risks in the world. Accenture is committed to bringing our deep OT security expertise to the organizations that protect the critical infrastructure communities depend on every day. This partnership will help put AI-powered defense in the hands of those who need it most.

In June,
we launched a cyber defense program
for state, local, tribal, and territorial governments. Since then, we’ve offered frontier Claude models and technical support to more than half of all US states and some of the country’s largest public critical infrastructure operators, speeding up code scanning and patching, incident response, red teaming, and other security workflows.
We are listening to and learning from the people who know this landscape best. Our approach is to work with the companies, coalitions, governments, and nonprofits that know this landscape and that operators trust, and provide support where it’s most needed.
Securing open-source software
Almost all software relies on open-source code, much of it maintained by small teams of volunteers. Under Project Glasswing, we scanned hundreds of widely used open-source projects, had humans triage and review many of the potential vulnerabilities uncovered, and privately reported what we found to their maintainers through our
coordinated vulnerability disclosure process
.
Some maintainers with the capacity to triage at scale asked us for everything our models had found in their project, reviewed or not. In response, we’re launching
OSS Scanner
, an opt-in service inspired by
Google’s OSS-Fuzz
. Enrolled projects receive periodic scans from our most capable models, free of charge. Each report includes a proof of concept of how the bug could be exploited, an explanation, and a suggested fix where one is available. The reports are model-generated and sent without human review. That means maintainers receive them faster, but it also means that some will contain inaccuracies, such as a wrong severity rating. We expect a true-positive rate above 90%, and will work to improve the true positive rate and fix quality over time. The
team’s post
explains how it works and how to enroll.
The service is meant for projects with the capacity to keep up with surfaced findings. For others, we will continue to share human-verified disclosures under our CVD policy.
OSS Scanner is a first step. From here, our open-source work aims to:
Get findings to maintainers faster.
Bring OSS Scanner to more projects while keeping human-verified disclosure for those that need it.
Accelerate fixes.
Automate triage and patching, which are still mostly manual, for projects that want it.
Explore new secure architectures and coding practices.
Research and share methods for hardening or rewriting code with projects that want to go further than patching.
We’ll do this based on guidance from open-source maintainers and foundations, and share what works so other projects can replicate it. We funded the organizations behind widely used open-source code, including the Python Software Foundation, Alpha-Omega and OpenSSF through the Linux Foundation, and the Apache Software Foundation, as well as supporting Akrites and Gold Eagle, which collect and coordinate vulnerability reports from many sources to avoid overwhelming maintainers. The Defender Advantage Fund (0xDAF), which we
launched in August
, supports pilot programs in these areas and keeps OSS Scanner free.
Maintainers can also apply to
Claude for Open Source
for free Claude Max subscriptions, and to the
Cyber Verification Program
for expanded access to Claude’s cyber capabilities for defensive work.
Why we're doing this
Highly cyber-capable AI models are widely available to attackers now. But defensive tools—including our own—have not yet reached enough of the defenders who need them.
OSS Scanner
, our
Cyber Verification Program
, defensive products our partners build on our platform, and
Claude Security
are some of our efforts here, and we’ll be adding others as soon as possible.
Our forecast is that in two years, AI will favor defense: it will be easier to catch bugs before they ship, write fundamentally secure software from scratch, and actively defend systems with models. But in the near term, that may not be true.
The cost of exploiting vulnerabilities has dropped
, while verifying, disclosing, and fixing them is slow and still depends on people. In Glasswing, we often saw months pass between a vulnerability being found and being fixed. With operational technology, a fix may have to wait until it can be applied safely to running machinery—in some rare cases, this might take decades.
Success means critical infrastructure such as water, power, transport, and communications keep running in the face of attacks by capable adversaries, with fewer exploitable paths in and faster recovery when something gets through. This will take years and we expect the Anthropic Cyber Mission to change as we, together with the public and private sector, learn what works.
The path ahead
Over the coming months, we’ll bring the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program to more partners and more sectors, and we’ll share what we learn along the way, including what didn’t work. We also expect other AI developers, security companies, and governments to run efforts of their own, and we’d like to collaborate with them wherever that helps defenders.
We will also expand our work to help secure open source and the broader supply chain. This includes researching new ways of writing software and new ways of defending systems. We intend to share frontier research, tools, and resources to help others secure their software and supply chain.
If you’d like to work with us:
Companies that build security products or services for critical infrastructure, including security vendors, system integrators, and equipment manufacturers, can register their interest in the
Critical Infrastructure Defense Program
as we expand it.
Core maintainers of critical open-source projects can
enroll in OSS Scanner
.
Security teams of any size, including operators of critical infrastructure and open-source maintainers, can
apply to our expanded Cyber Verification Program
for access to our models.

NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark

User-defined functions in Spark break the declarative abstraction, forcing GPU-accelerated pipelines to fall back to CPU execution and incur data transfer overhead.
UDFs can be rewritten using Spark SQL expressions, the RapidsUDF interface with the
Java API for cuDF

The
cuDF skills for Apache Spark
provide agent-driven workflows that guide testing, conversion, benchmarking, and optimization with verification-driven feedback loops.
A major consumer technology company converted more than 30 production UDFs using this workflow, with one rewrite reducing operator time from 274.55 to 12.78 hours across a 600-billion-row workload.

Learn more
Enterprise applications have become increasingly demanding. Agentic AI has compounded the need for vast amounts of enterprise data with frequent, complex queries across increasingly large datasets.
Meeting that demand requires greater data throughput without a proportional increase in cost.
NVIDIA cuDF
addresses this challenge by leveraging the massive parallelism and high-bandwidth memory of GPUs for data analytics. Particularly, the
NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark
brings this acceleration to
Apache Spark
, the industry-leading platform for big data processing and analytics, to achieve
better TCO performance
in major workloads.
User-defined functions (UDFs)
have long been problematic for accelerated query engines,
introducing runtime overheads due to their opaque nature. While UDFs can often be replaced with more performant code, rewriting UDFs has long been a laborious process requiring careful validation.
This post describes how to use agents to rewrite UDFs into GPU-accelerated equivalents within minutes, achieving 22x+ speedups in Apache Spark jobs
. We’ll introduce the
cuDF skills for Apache Spark
, a set of skills to quickly break through the UDF bottleneck for end-to-end development, from testing, to benchmarking, through integration.
The UDF challenge
cuDF achieves seamless GPU acceleration in part due to Apache Spark’s declarative programming interface. The SQL / Dataframe abstractions are powerful because they separate what a query should produce from how the system should execute it. This enables the cuDF plugin to transparently parallelize row-wise operations using the massive
SIMD
capabilities of GPUs, without any change in user code.
Apache Spark, however, also supports UDFs: custom routines to extend built-in functionality. While useful for implementing bespoke business logic, UDFs break the declarative abstraction—they contain arbitrary user code which the system cannot reason about or parallelize in any general sense. During execution, the GPU accelerator must convert the data from a columnar to row-wise format, and fall back to the CPU to execute the UDF row-by-row:
Figure 1.A CPU UDF forces an otherwise GPU-resident pipeline to convert columnar batches to rows, execute on the CPU, and convert back to columnar format
Thus in an otherwise accelerated query, UDFs have the following drawbacks:
The UDF incurs a round-trip data transfer overhead due to fallback.
The UDF forgoes potential compute speedup, had it been written using GPU-accelerated primitives.
Accelerating UDFs
With a small, targeted code change, many UDFs can be rewritten into a GPU-accelerable form by using the right primitives. Rewriting UDFs eliminates the overhead associated with accelerator fallback, and can yield speedups of
over 20x
.
We outline three approaches to rewrite UDFs:
Approach
Complexity
Best For
SQL
Low, highest level of abstraction
Simple relational logic, e.g. small or inlined functions
cuDF
Medium, more flexibility and control over execution
Most cases, e.g. moderately complex logic like string parsing, nested types
CUDA
High, maximum flexibility and kernel-level control
Most complex or performance critical logic
Table 1. Comparison of SQL, cuDF, and CUDA approaches for rewriting Spark UDFs, organized by complexity and best-fit use case
To make these approaches concrete, consider a simple Scala UDF that converts temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit:
final class ToFahrenheit
extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double]
with Serializable {
override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = {
if (celsius == null) null
else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
}
}
spark.udf.register("to_fahrenheit", new ToFahrenheit)
spark.sql("""
SELECT
*,
to_fahrenheit(celsius) AS fahrenheit
FROM temperatures
""")
Rewriting the UDF with SQL
The most direct solution for simple UDFs is to replace the UDF with an equivalent Spark SQL expression:
spark.sql("""
SELECT
*,
celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 AS fahrenheit
FROM temperatures
""")
This makes the function visible in Spark’s expression tree. During query planning, the cuDF plugin will replace these expressions with their corresponding GPU implementations, keeping the data and execution fully on the GPU.
Rewriting the UDF with cuDF
When SQL primitives are insufficient or undesirable, the UDF can instead operate directly on GPU columns using the
RapidsUDF
interface, a contract provided by the cuDF plugin. The contract requires a single method,
evaluateColumnar
:
import ai.rapids.cudf.{ColumnVector, Scalar}
import com.nvidia.spark.RapidsUDF
import scala.util.Using
final class ToFahrenheit
extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double]
with Serializable
with RapidsUDF {
override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = {
if (celsius == null) null
else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
}
override def evaluateColumnar(
numRows: Int,
args: ColumnVector*): ColumnVector = {
Using.Manager { use =>
val scale = use(Scalar.fromDouble(9.0 / 5.0))
val offset = use(Scalar.fromDouble(32.0))
val scaled = use(args.head.mul(scale))
scaled.add(offset)
}.get
}
}
The cuDF plugin recognizes instances of the
RapidsUDF
interface and passes a GPU-resident
ColumnVector
to the
evaluateColumnar
function. The function then composes operations from the
Java API for cuDF
operations to process the column in parallel. This approach provides a richer API for more complex processing.
Rewriting the UDF with CUDA
For highly complex logic that cannot be efficiently composed from existing cuDF operations, a
RapidsUDF
can invoke a custom CUDA kernel through the
Java Native Interface (JNI)
. We’ve elided the code for brevity, but examples of CUDA conversions can be found in the
cuDF examples for Spark UDFs
.
Efficient rewrites with AI agents
Despite the performance benefits, UDF rewrites can require significant engineering effort. They demand careful API selection, semantic validation, and performance measurement, while columnar APIs can be unfamiliar to practitioners with less experience in vectorized programming.
Fortunately, much of this work is well suited to coding agents. With proper guardrails, an agent can search unfamiliar APIs, implement candidate rewrites, and iterate quickly while executable tests and performance measurements determine whether each change is acceptable.
Available skills
The cuDF skills for Apache Spark decompose the rewrite into four focused feedback loops. Each skill defines both the work to perform and the evidence required before proceeding to the next stage:
Figure 2. Four skills guide agents through testing, conversion, benchmarking, and optimization, with verification-driven feedback loops at each stage
Scaffolding and design
Reliable agent execution begins with a reliable development environment. The skills provide a complete project template containing the cuDF- and Spark-specific scaffolding required for end-to-end development. This includes test and benchmark harnesses, encoded routines for output verification, and build configuration. By encoding this knowledge into code, the agent can focus on the UDF rather than repeatedly reconstructing specialized infrastructure.
The skills also provide best practices for GPU programming with cuDF, including memory management and configuration. This serves as an advisory tips and tricks reference. To best leverage the power of frontier models, the agent remains free to explore different implementations based on surrounding context and select an approach based on measured correctness and performance.
Performance results
A major consumer technology company used this workflow to convert 30+ UDFs used in production data pipelines into GPU-accelerated implementations. The rewrites preserved the behavior of the original CPU UDFs while removing costly fallbacks from otherwise GPU-accelerated workloads. As an example, the following benchmark shows the resulting before-and-after performance for a UDF in one such workload:
Figure 3. Rewriting a production CPU-based UDF with cuDF reduced operator time from 274.55 to 12.78 hours, a 22x speedup across a 600-billion-row workload
This particular UDF was affecting
more than 3,000+ jobs
, and in this job,
saw a 22x speedup
when implemented as a cuDF-enabled RapidsUDF. With the help of agents, these performance gains are much more attainable, enabling practitioners to iterate on rewrites on the order of hours rather than days or weeks, without compromising correctness.
Get started
Converting UDFs to GPU implementations can unlock major speedups and contribute to overall cost savings in GPU-accelerated pipelines. With agent skills, the rewrite process can be made both
easy and reliable.
To get started, install the
cuDF skills for Apache Spark on GitHub
, either directly or using the
npx
skill installer:
npx skills add NVIDIA/cudf-spark --skill ‘*’
For a deeper walkthrough of the workflow and practical lessons from building it, see the Data + AI Summit session,
Coding with AI Agents to Supercharge Your Spark UDFs with GPU Acceleration
.
To learn more about GPU acceleration for Apache Spark, follow the
cuDF plugin for Apache Spark getting-started guide
to unlock better performance and TCO across your Spark pipelines. Visit our webpage to learn more about
NVIDIA cuDF: GPU-Accelerated Structured Data Processing
, or you can read the docs for more information on
NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark
.

NVIDIA Run:ai Is Now Open Source as Part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform
Accelerate innovation across the DSX ecosystem and bring AI factory solutions to market faster with the open foundation for AI workload and GPU orchestration.
Oct 13, 2026
By
Ekin Karabulut
and
Sam Heywood

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA is releasing the full
NVIDIA Run:ai
platform as open source software, expanding the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform with a foundation for AI workload and GPU orchestration.
The release includes four modular components that can be adopted independently:
KAI Scheduler
for GPU-aware Kubernetes scheduling, GPU Fractioning Operator for CUDA-native GPU sharing, KAI Resource Management for organizational quota and hierarchy, and Workload Map for a consistent workload-management contract.
Eight NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners including Crusoe, Mirantis, Nebius, OpenNebula Systems, Rafay, Saturn Cloud, Spectro Cloud, and vCluster are integrating the open source platform into their offerings.
Related open source projects Model Streamer and Grove complement the platform by accelerating model loading and orchestrating multicomponent inference workloads.
Next Steps
Explore the
NVIDIA Run:ai
full platform repository to inspect code and begin adoption.
Review the
KAI Scheduler
project for GPU-aware Kubernetes scheduling capabilities.
Try the
GPU Fractioning Operator
to enable CUDA-native GPU fractions on Kubernetes clusters.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
NVIDIA is making the full
NVIDIA Run:ai
platform available as open source software, giving customers, developers, and ecosystem partners access to production-grade AI workload and GPU orchestration capabilities. This release expands the
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform
by establishing NVIDIA Run:ai as an open foundation that enables the broader ecosystem to bring differentiated solutions to market faster in response to evolving customer needs.
Over the past several years, NVIDIA Run:ai has helped organizations run AI workloads on Kubernetes at scale by dynamically allocating GPU resources and managing workloads across the full lifecycle, from data processing and training to inference.
By open sourcing NVIDIA Run:ai platform capabilities as part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory, it is now possible for every NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner and AI cloud to increase workload throughput, improve GPU utilization, and operate shared AI infrastructure more efficiently and effectively.
This post details the open source release, which includes the complete
NVIDIA Run:ai platform
and four components that can also be adopted independently:
KAI Scheduler,
GPU Fractioning Operator
,
KAI Resource Management
,
Workload Map
. Together with additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. Platform teams and ecosystem partners can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole, build on it for their own products and services, or integrate individual components based on their requirements.
How to adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai
NVIDIA Run:ai can be adopted directly as open-source software or through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner offerings.
Deploy the open source platform directly
The complete source code for NVIDIA Run:ai is available in the
NVIDIA Run:ai repository
within the
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization
. Teams can inspect the code, contribute to its development, build on top of the platform or adopt its modular components independently.
The complete open source NVIDIA Run:ai platform is also available on
NVIDIA NGC
as a Community Product, with a Helm chart for installing the integrated stack.
Note: The NVIDIA Run:ai source code is governed by its applicable open source licenses. Downloading the Community Product from NGC requires acceptance of the applicable NVIDIA Software License Agreement and Product-Specific Terms for NVIDIA AI Products. No paid NVIDIA Run:ai subscription or NVIDIA support entitlement is required for the Community Product, and NVIDIA enterprise support is not included.
Adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners
Open source NVIDIA Run:ai gives NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners direct access to AI workload and GPU orchestration innovations they can use in their own NVIDIA DSX AI factory solutions. By adopting the complete platform or integrating individual components, partners can bring those innovations to market faster and respond more quickly to evolving customer and operational requirements.
Crusoe
integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with Crusoe Managed Kubernetes, combining GPU workload orchestration with managed Kubernetes and GPU infrastructure.
Mirantis
extends k0rdent AI with NVIDIA Run:ai to deliver a lifecycle-managed, Metal-to-Model AI factory stack that automates infrastructure provisioning and maximizes GPU utilization.
Nebius
offers NVIDIA Run:ai as a one-click application deployment in Nebius AI Cloud, giving customers a streamlined way to deploy and operate the complete platform on Nebius Managed Service for Kubernetes.
OpenNebula
Systems integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with the OpenNebula AI Cloud Platform through OneKS, combining GPU workload orchestration with infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management for open and sovereign AI clouds.
Rafay
is expanding its NVIDIA Run:ai integration to deliver it as a fully managed service. Rafay automates the entire stack, from GPU infrastructure and clusters to the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and tenants, so AI cloud providers and enterprises can offer it through their own self-service catalogs.
Saturn Cloud
integrates NVIDIA Run:ai to help AI cloud operators launch white-label AI inference services through its Token Factory platform, combining GPU orchestration with dedicated and multi-tenant model serving, per-token metering, and automated billing.
Spectro Cloud
integrates NVIDIA Run:ai into PaletteAI, enabling customers to deploy it through PaletteAI Studio and manage it with the same lifecycle automation used across their AI infrastructure.
vCluster
provides NVIDIA Run:ai through pre-validated deployment templates that stand up a complete environment per tenant, allowing operators to strengthen tenant boundaries while NVIDIA Run:ai continues to schedule across one GPU fleet.
For NVIDIA Enterprise AI Factory deployments, NVIDIA Run:ai continues to be available through NVIDIA-supported commercial offerings including as a standalone product, through NVIDIA Mission Control and NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and select cloud marketplaces. Availability, licensing, and support terms vary by offering.
For teams that already have a platform and need to fill a specific capability gap, the following sections describe when and how to use each modular component independently.
Modular open source components of the NVIDIA Run:ai platform
This section details the four components included in the open source release: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, and Workload Map. With additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. You can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole or integrate individual components based on your unique requirements.
KAI Scheduler: The scheduling engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai
KAI Scheduler
is the Kubernetes-native scheduler that powers the NVIDIA Run:ai platform. NVIDIA released KAI Scheduler as open source software under the Apache 2.0 license and
contributed it to CNCF
as a Sandbox project. KAI remains the upstream engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai, and all scheduler development happens in the community repository, so every improvement flows through the same codebase. NVIDIA continues to support the project’s maintainers and work with the broader ecosystem to advance AI workload scheduling at scale.
KAI Scheduler is purpose-built for GPU workloads at scale, coordinating:
Gang scheduling with prescheduling in-memory simulation, so multipod jobs are placed all-or-nothing and aren’t evicted needlessly
Fair-share (including time-based fair-share) and quota allocation that keeps resource shares balanced across teams
Topology awareness and bin-packing at the scheduling-decision level
GPU sharing, which allows multiple workloads to share single or multiple GPUs (MIG, MPS, time sharing, HaMi, CUDA 13.4 MPS fractioning)
Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) support
To learn more about key features, visit the
kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler
GitHub repo.
Use KAI Scheduler for diverse AI workloads that require fair access to cluster resources and topology-aware placement. It can be deployed in an existing cluster alongside the current software stack without requiring the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform.
Follow the project, ask questions in the #kai-scheduler channel on CNCF Slack, and contribute on the
kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler
GitHub repo.
GPU Fractioning: An operator for GPU fractions on Kubernetes
The NVIDIA Run:ai platform has long supported fractional GPU allocation, enabling multiple workloads to share a GPU with hard memory isolation. Fractions can be requested on demand and set up on the fly, with no per-node setup from an administrator in advance. It is one of the most widely used capabilities among ML teams running workloads that do not require the full memory of a GPU, including interactive notebooks and inference for smaller models. NVIDIA Run:ai pioneered that experience with a proprietary implementation.
GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and the proprietary implementation has been retired in favor of the native capability available in
CUDA 13.4
.
The CUDA driver enforces a hard limit on GPU memory for each workload, and each workload sees only the GPU memory allocated to its fraction. What is still needed is a clean way to consume it on Kubernetes. This is what
GPU Fractioning Operator
provides: an operator that enables CUDA GPU fractions on a cluster, along with a metrics exporter for per-pod visibility into fractions in use. It is a Kubernetes integration layer that allows workloads to use CUDA-native fractioning, and it is scheduler-agnostic.
Use the GPU Fractioning Operator for workloads that can share underutilized GPU capacity, including notebooks, development sessions, and smaller models. GPU Fractioning Operator integrates with KAI Scheduler to translate available GPU capacity into an actual placement decision, while remaining compatible with other schedulers.
GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA 13.4-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and integrates with KAI Scheduler. To get started, refer to the
GPU Fractioning Operator documentation
.
KAI Resource Management: The organizational layer
While the scheduler decides how work is placed,
KAI Resource Management
governs who gets what:
Projects and departments:
The organizational structure, or “org layer,” that maps resources to the teams and initiatives that consume them.
Resource management with an organizational hierarchy:
The ability to allocate, guarantee, and share GPU capacity across that org structure, with fair-share and quota semantics.
Node pools:
Grouping and targeting of heterogeneous hardware so workloads land on the right resources.
Together, these let platform teams move beyond raw Kubernetes scheduling and manage GPUs the way organizations actually operate: by team, by department, by initiative, and by resource guarantee.
Use KAI Resource Management for heterogeneous clusters shared by multiple teams that require defined shares of capacity. For example, a platform team could guarantee 50% of the cluster to research while preventing any one team from monopolizing the remaining capacity. If you are already tracking quota entitlements in a spreadsheet or hand-maintaining namespaces per team, this is the layer that replaces it. It can be combined with KAI Scheduler in your clusters.
Read more about how these concepts map to real deployments in the
KAI Resource Management documentation
.
Workload Map: A workload-management contract for Kubernetes
Workload Map
is the contract NVIDIA Run:ai uses to support any workload type. KAI Scheduler uses it for scheduling and gang semantics; the rest of the platform uses it for workload discovery, monitoring and lifecycle management.
In Kubernetes, an AI workload is almost never a bare Deployment or Job. It is a PyTorchJob, a RayCluster, a JobSet, a KServe InferenceService, a Dynamo graph deployment, or a company’s own custom resource. Each type has its own internal structure, components with different roles (driver and workers, head and workers, prefill and decode), its own scaling and gang semantics, and its own way of reporting status.
Workload Map provides a consistent way to treat these workloads as first-class objects throughout their lifecycle:
Describing pods, components, and roles
Submitting and configuring
Scheduling with gang and topology awareness
Observing status and health consistently
Applying policy at admission or runtime
This workload-management layer sits between Kubernetes primitives and the schedulers, dashboards, SRE and troubleshooting tools, cost tools, backup tools, and ML platforms that serve users. Instead of each tool building a private, partial integration for every CRD, Workload Map defines each workload type once so any platform or tool can schedule, observe, act on, and govern it consistently without hardcoding each CRD.
Use Workload Map for platforms and tools that must understand and manage multiple Kubernetes workload types without hardcoding each CRD. It ships as a Go library that works offline on unstructured objects, so you can adopt it without adding anything to your cluster. It is deliberately narrow: Workload Map describes workload structure and does not schedule, queue, autoscale, or propagate across clusters.
Learn more in the
dsx-ai-factory/workload-map
GitHub repo and check out the
adopter projects
.
Related open source platform software
The following open source projects address complementary AI infrastructure challenges. They can be adopted independently or incorporated into broader solutions that include the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform or selected components.
Model Streamer: Reducing cold-start latency
Cold-starting an inference workload on Kubernetes can take several minutes, during which time GPUs are allocated but idle for a single step: loading model weights from storage onto the GPU. Model Streamer reads weights concurrently and streams them directly into GPU memory, cutting load time for large models.
Since its release, Model Streamer has been adopted across the inference stack, including by inference engines, cloud providers and storage platform vendors.
Inference engines
Model Streamer is integrated upstream in
vLLM
and
SGLang
, where it can be enabled with the
--load-format runai_streamer
flag, as well as in
ModelExpress
. Support covers local filesystems, S3-compatible stores, and network file shares alongside several cloud backends detailed below.
Clouds
Major cloud providers now document Model Streamer in their own guidance.
AWS
: Model Streamer ships in the
vLLM Deep Learning Container
and is the recommended fast path in the official
EKS documentation for running AI/ML inference
, with
tuned concurrency and chunk sizing for S3
.
Google Cloud
:
Native Cloud Storage support built in collaboration with NVIDIA
, including
GKE documentation
for streaming straight from a bucket into accelerator memory.
Microsoft Azure
: Azure Blob Storage integration, jointly developed by Microsoft and NVIDIA Run:ai to provide first-class model streaming for Azure customers.
Published benchmarks
on eight NVIDIA H100 VMs shows 3x-6x faster loading than the default loader and a steady 80 Gbps, compared with approximately 40 Gbps for the default path.
Storage platforms
Several AI data infrastructure partners have independently benchmarked Model Streamer and published their results:
WEKA
loaded into GPU memory in just 3.5 seconds, roughly 40% faster than loading from local NVMe—enabling organizations to build petabyte-scale shared model repositories that accelerate model readiness without the time, effort, and capacity required to maintain duplicate model copies across the inference environment.
VAST Data measured measured 1.7 seconds, a 60% improvement over loading from local NVMe
DDN
streamed the 65.5 GB Qwen3-32B across 8 GPUs in under four seconds, and translated it into cost: saving up to 10% of daily GPU runtime compared to using local storage.
Use Model Streamer when starting new replicas and loading model weights is the primary bottleneck.
Grove: One API, any inference architecture
Emerging workload patterns—including agentic pipelines, disaggregated serving and mixture-of-experts training—consist of multiple connected components that must scale together. Grove provides a Kubernetes API for orchestrating these workloads, from a single pod to deployments spanning tens of thousands of GPUs.
Grove provides topology-aware autoscaling and hierarchical gang scheduling, allowing components such as prefill and decode to start as all-or-nothing units. On
NVIDIA GB200 NVL72
, it also manages ComputeDomain resources automatically, enabling multinode NVLink performance through a single annotation instead of hand-authored YAML.
Grove is a modular part of
NVIDIA Dynamo
that can be used independently, and it already powers training and inference pipelines at scale across a range of companies. Recent work includes support for llm-d and Volcano as a scheduler backend, with Kueue support in progress.
Use Grove for graph-based workloads with distinct roles and coupled scaling requirements.
Get started with open source NVIDIA Run:ai
NVIDIA Run:ai is available now as open source software in the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. To learn more and get started, check out these resources:
NVIDIA Run:ai
full platform
KAI Scheduler
scheduling engine
KAI Resource Management
for projects, departments, quotas, and node pools
GPU Fractioning Operator
for CUDA GPU fractions on Kubernetes, with per-pod metrics
Workload Map
workload-management contract
Related open source projects include:
Model Streamer

Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
- Google Developers Blog
Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
OCT. 13, 2026
Kanishka Rao
Principal Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI.
You can see this leap in capability on the
Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark
, which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model.
As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas:
Robot control →

When a new model launches, most demos show greenfield apps built from an empty folder. They're fun to watch. They also tell a working software engineer very little about how the model handles an existing codebase.
For the launch of Gemini 4 Argon, we wanted to test whether it could run unattended overnight on a much harder problem: finding and fixing cross-file performance bottlenecks in
google/adk-python
. Agent Development Kit (ADK) is Google's open-source framework for building and deploying enterprise agents.
The Python repository spans roughly 205,000 lines of code across nearly 800 source files, backed by nearly 17,000 unit tests.
Performance work is a hard test for a model because you can't just open one file and spot the slowdown. You have to look orthogonally to where the symptom appears and hold a map of how the entire codebase fits together over a long run.
This post walks through the prompts,
.agents/skills
rulefiles, and human code-review decisions from the 11-hour overnight run that cut ADK's in-memory session prep time by about 40% in long sessions and sped up cold package imports by 21%. You'll see the two optimizations that shipped, the four we rejected in review, and how to set up the same overnight workflow on your own codebase.
Figure 1: ADK's overhead before the first model request, measured after 50 and 150 turns. Argon's change cuts it by about 40% at both points, so the time saved grows as the session gets longer.
Steering the run with .agents/skills and /goal mode
Most performance work with a coding agent still runs in a tight human loop: an engineer runs a profiler, points the model at a single hot function, and specifies the fix. We wanted to see what Argon would do when given only the outcome the team cared about.
In round one, we tested Argon with zero custom repository instructions. We gave it this single-paragraph prompt:
Make ADK add no noticeable overhead to any agent:
at startup, in long sessions, in multi-agent and
workflow setups. Keep what the model receives and
the public API unchanged, and back each change
with a test that would catch a regression.
Round one ran for about two hours. Argon wrote a benchmark script 7 minutes in, spent 70 minutes measuring and reading code before editing a single line of ADK source, and found real bottlenecks in session copying and package imports. Parts of round one's code made it into the
final commit
we shipped.
Where round one fell short was maintainer conventions. Because Argon didn't know how the ADK team reviews code, it attached a custom hook to ADK's authentication model that subtly altered its public JSON schema, missed mock event edge cases in its custom copier, ran only 216 nearby unit tests, and left benchmark numbers out of its pull request description.
Round one proved there were real speedups to be had, so we set up a second round with two adjustments. First, we put the team's maintainer guidelines into the repository's
.agents/skills
directory, like an onboarding guide for a new engineer. Each skill starts with a short
SKILL.md
index that points to focused
references/
files on demand, so we don't flood the agent's context window on every turn. When Argon started its run at 9:11 PM (Figure 2), it read
visibility.md
for our private
_-prefixed
module rule and
imports.md
for our lazy-loading checks before touching a line of code.
Figure 2: Argon's two-hour first run compared with its 11-hour overnight run on the same goal. Round 1 found real speedups on its own, while Round 2 followed repo conventions, ran all 16,892 unit tests, and opened a review-ready pull request.
Second, we turned on /goal mode in
Google Antigravity
, which preserves the goal across context compactions so the agent keeps running until the task is finished. We also added two sentences asking for an unmerged pull request with before-and-after numbers:
/goal Make ADK add no noticeable overhead to any agent:
at startup, in long sessions, in multi-agent and workflow setups.
Keep what the model receives and the public API unchanged, and back each change with a test that would catch a regression.
Open one pull request against main that the ADK maintainers would approve, with before and after numbers in its description. Don't merge it.
With .agents/skills in the repo and /goal mode active, Argon ran unattended for 11 hours overnight (Figure 3).
Figure 3: Argon's overnight ADK run in Google Antigravity. The /goal prompt stays pinned at the top and bottom of the window while finished work collapses into summary blocks, so the original rules stay in view across hours of edits, benchmarks, and test runs. (Screenshot replayed in the public Antigravity interface to remove internal workspace details.)
6 proposals led to 2 shipped changes after code review
Looking at the overnight session log the next morning, a few behaviors stood out right away. Before touching source code, Argon read 12 guideline files and ran a baseline benchmark across four test workloads: package startup, a 200-step conversation, a test app where 20 sub-agents hand tasks to one another, and a 12-node workflow, run 30 times. Even three minutes before finishing its 11-hour run, Argon was still auditing its own diff, catching a bug in its own multi-agent cache and rerunning all 16,892 unit tests before stopping on its own.
More importantly, Argon did the cross-module legwork a profiler can't do for you. A profiler will tell you that copying sessions and importing packages take time. What it won't do is trace every caller, mock target, and shared reference across 40 files so that speeding up those paths doesn't break existing apps.
In total, Argon's pull request proposed six optimizations across 32 files. Two of those optimizations solved ADK's core bottlenecks cleanly and shipped to production:
1. Filtering in-memory session history before copying
Every step in an ADK run starts by loading the conversation history. Previously, ADK's in-memory session service deep-copied the entire stored conversation on every read before filtering down to the events a caller asked for. Even listing sessions without their events copied every event first. Argon updated the service to filter events before copying, and replaced Pydantic's generic deep-copy path on sessions and events with a fast, cycle-safe copier that preserves shared state dictionaries and test mocks.
2. Loading heavy packages only when needed
Running
import google.adk
previously pulled in modules for live audio and video streaming, OpenTelemetry tracing, and web servers (FastAPI and Starlette) even for a basic text agent. Simply deleting top-level imports in a framework breaks downstream tests that mock attributes directly on modules. When Argon's round-two pull request removed three internal flow imports from
llm_agent.py
, all 16,892 open-source tests passed, yet 25 internal Google test targets failed because they patched those exact attributes. The shipped fix uses lazy module accessors so heavy packages load only on first use while every public attribute stays patchable where tests expect it.
What about the other four optimizations Argon proposed?
We found that the model comes up with creative solutions we wouldn’t have considered otherwise. Some of those creative ideas run into framework rules where breaking changes are not acceptable.
Figure 4: The six optimizations in Argon's morning pull request, split between the two we shipped and the four we cut in code review. We kept the session-copy and lazy-import changes that cut real overhead cleanly, and dropped the four that relied on fragile state, private library internals, or synthetic-only gains.
During code review, we rejected the other four changes:
A multi-agent event cache sped up a synthetic benchmark by 17%, yet relied on a weak memory reference that could return stale data across sessions if Python reused a memory address after garbage collection.
A telemetry check read a private attribute on OpenTelemetry's tracer implementation, which could break silently on a minor library upgrade.
A rewrite of how ADK formats conversation history before each model call made a core code path harder to read without moving end-to-end latency on our independent holdout benchmark.
A lookup index for workflow event replays added state-tracking complexity that only helped synthetic replay tests rather than everyday agent runs.
That division of labor is why the workflow worked:
the agent explores, the maintainer subtracts
. We combined the best parts of rounds one and two into a 22-file change backed by 17 new test functions. After review across the ADK team, it landed in main with the commit note "Argon generated these changes."
Benchmark results: what a "turn" is in ADK, and why 158 turns matters
To make sense of the numbers in the commit message, it helps to know what ADK calls a turn.
When an engineer types a prompt and gets a final answer back, ADK calls that an invocation. A turn is an internal step under the hood every time the agent acts: calling a tool, running a batch of parallel tool calls, or querying an MCP server.
The reason you use an agent framework is multi-turn tool calling, where dozens or hundreds of internal turns happen underneath a run.
Before either round ran we wrote an independent holdout benchmark (bench_turn.py) that Argon never saw. In bench_turn.py, a single session grows turn by turn against an instant model and instant tools, so every millisecond on the clock is ADK's own framework overhead. Each turn runs three rounds of four parallel tool calls before returning its answer, timing 5 turns after 0, 50, and 150 earlier turns. Each number below is the median of 6 to 12 runs, and on every turn the model receives byte-identical requests before and after the change.
We tested the merged commit against the previous release across five benchmarks (Figure 5):
Figure 5: Median ADK framework overhead before and after Argon's changes across all five holdout benchmarks. Session preparation drops by about 40% in long sessions and package import time drops by 21%, while new-process time to first request stays flat because deferred modules load on the first turn.
How to read these numbers for your own agents:
The 21% faster import google.adk helps every ADK user right away, speeding up CLI commands, local development, and test discovery. Because deferred modules still load when an agent runs its first turn, time from a brand-new process to its first model request stays flat (3.07 s to 3.09 s). On a production server, send a warm-up request before taking live traffic so the first user call doesn't pay that one-time import cost.
The 40% reduction in pre-model overhead applies to
InMemorySessionService
, which powers
InMemoryRunner
, local evaluation loops, CI test suites, and default Cloud Run or GKE deployments when no external database URI is configured. On a single LLM call that takes seconds, a human won't feel 28 ms or 78 ms. Across 158 internal turns of tool calling interactions, however, those copies compound: removing them
cuts the full 158-turn run from 65.6 seconds to 56.1 seconds
(nearly 10 seconds of pure framework overhead). External database, SQLite, Gemini platform, Firestore, and Redis session stores deserialize from storage rather than deep-copying in memory, so their read times don't change here.
Try Gemini 4 Argon
Enterprise developers and builders can access Argon via API in
Gemini platform
under model ID
gemini-4-argon
, in
Google AI Studio
, and in
Google Antigravity
.
Review the
model card
and
developer guide
for complete technical specifications, token limits, and migration instructions.

merged pull request and benchmark commit
directly in
